Footstool
foot´stool
n. (a stool for the feet; in Scripture, the earth, the ark, and the place of subdued enemies; rendering Hebrew hadom, Greek hupopodion)
A plain English compound. Scripture makes it one of its largest images: what is beneath the feet of a seated King.

Biblical Definition

Footstool is a throne-word. Because a king sits and rests his feet, whatever is his footstool is both near him and under him — and Scripture assigns three things to that position. The earth itself: “The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: where is the house that ye build unto me?” (Isa 66:1), which permanently forbids any theology that houses God in a building. The ark and the sanctuary: David calls the ark “the footstool of our God” (1Ch 28:2), and the Psalter summons the congregation to “worship at his footstool; for he is holy” (Psa 99:5) — worship is offered at the feet, never at the level of the throne. And His enemies: “Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool” (Psa 110:1), the most-quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament, and the Bible's definitive statement of the reign of Christ between the ascension and the end.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a footstool simply as a stool for the feet, that on which the feet rest when sitting — and notes the Scriptural use for the earth and for subdued enemies.

Key Scripture

Psa 110:1 — "A Psalm of David. The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool."

Isa 66:1 — "Thus saith the LORD, The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: where is the house that ye build unto me? and where is the place of my rest?"

Psa 99:5 — "Exalt ye the LORD our God, and worship at his footstool; for he is holy."

1Ch 28:2 — "Then David the king stood up upon his feet, and said, Hear me, my brethren, and my people: As for me, I had in mine heart to build an house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and for the footstool of our God, and had made ready for the building:"

Modern Corruption

An over-realized triumphalism that treats the enemies as already underfoot, and an under-realized despair that doubts they ever will be — both misread the single word until.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The errors here are internal to the church and both turn on Psalm 110:1. One party reads the subjugation as finished and expects a Christendom without opposition, and is scandalized by every setback. The other reads the delay as doubt and expects only defeat until the end. The verse holds a precise middle: Christ is already seated at the right hand, which is the language of accomplished authority, and the enemies are being made His footstool, which is the language of a process with a term. He reigns now; the subduing is under way.

Isaiah 66:1 supplies the principle to recover for worship. If the earth is merely God's footstool, then no building contains Him and no institution manages Him, and the question where is the house that ye build unto me? is aimed at religious presumption in every age. Psalm 99:5 then shows the only fitting posture: worship at the footstool, low, on the ground — and the reason given is not sentiment but holiness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew hadom (H1916), a footstool — used only with raglayim, feet; Greek hupopodion (G5286), literally under-foot-thing, the word in every New Testament citation of Psalm 110.

expand to see more

Hebrew hadom (H1916) — footstool; applied to the ark (1Ch 28:2), the sanctuary (Psa 132:7), and the earth (Isa 66:1).

Greek hupopodion (G5286) — a footstool, that under the feet; Heb 1:13 and Heb 10:13 press the until of Psa 110:1.

Hebrew hadom raglai — the footstool of my feet; the full idiom, emphasizing nearness as well as subjection.

Usage

"“Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool” — seated now, subduing still."

"“The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool” — no building contains Him."

"“Worship at his footstool; for he is holy” — the posture is low, and the reason is holiness."
